label: Compact Surfaces
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 159 through 182 and builds the classification theorem for compact connected surfaces. We translate continuous topology into finite combinatorics: every such surface is assembled from an edge-paired polygon, and two simple invariants will eventually pin down exactly which standard model it is.

label: Polygonal Presentations
notes: A polygonal presentation is a disk whose boundary edges are named and paired, then glued by affine maps. The cyclic edge word records the gluing recipe. Each label appears exactly twice, and the quotient is locally Euclidean everywhere, even where many polygon corners fuse into one point.

label: Reading a Schema
notes: From an edge word we extract finite data: one two-cell, one one-cell per label pair, and vertex classes found by union-find on the corners. Counting these gives the Euler characteristic directly. The torus word a b a-inverse b-inverse identifies all four corners to a single vertex.

label: Orientability
notes: Orientability is a combinatorial flag in this model. A pair is complementary when its label appears once forward and once reversed, and twisted when both occurrences run the same way. A presentation is orientable exactly when no pair is twisted, so a consistent face orientation survives all gluings.

label: The Standard Surfaces
notes: The standard list has three columns: the sphere with word a a-inverse, the orientable genus-g surface built from g commutator handle blocks, and the nonorientable surface built from k twisted crosscap pairs. Every compact connected surface, the theorem promises, is homeomorphic to exactly one of these models.

label: Connected Sum
notes: Connected sum removes an open disk from each surface and glues the resulting boundary circles. For one-face presentations this is just concatenating the two edge words over disjoint alphabets. Geometrically it splices two surfaces into one, and it is the operation that manufactures every higher-genus member of the list.

label: Genus-2 by Connected Sum
notes: Two tori, each cut along a small circle, glue along those circles to produce the genus-two surface with two handles. The edge word becomes the two commutator blocks written in sequence. This picture is the prototype: adding a handle is exactly adding one more commutator block to the presentation word.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: The Euler characteristic V minus E plus F is the chapter's first fast invariant. Elementary transformations on a presentation change vertex, edge, and face counts in amounts that always cancel, so chi is preserved. Connected sum subtracts two each time, which is exactly how each handle or crosscap lowers chi.

label: The Two Formulas
notes: For the standard families the Euler characteristic collapses to two clean formulas: chi equals two minus two g for the orientable genus-g surface, and chi equals two minus k for the connected sum of k projective planes. Genus or crosscap count is therefore recoverable directly from chi.

label: Klein Bottle and Crosscaps
notes: The Klein bottle, word a b a b-inverse, is nonorientable with Euler characteristic zero, and a cutting argument shows it equals the connected sum of two projective planes. Likewise a torus summed with a projective plane equals three projective planes, so no mixed orientable-nonorientable family is ever needed.

label: The Classification Theorem
notes: The proof is a reduction algorithm. Triangulate, paste into one face, cancel adjacent complementary pairs, gather twisted pairs, consolidate the vertices to one class, and isolate commutator handle blocks. The result is always a sphere, a sum of tori, or a sum of projective planes, exhausting the standard list.

label: Invariants and Outlook
notes: Euler characteristic plus orientability together separate the standard surfaces at the presentation level: chi zero with orientability is the torus, chi zero without it is the Klein bottle. Chapter ten supplies the homology that proves these invariants are genuinely topological, completing the classification's distinctness claim.
